summary: Reviewed the dvpwa (Damn Vulnerable Python Web Application) aiohttp project in full: the views, DAO layer, auth utilities, middlewares, templates, service setup, config, SQL migrations and Docker/compose files. The application is intentionally vulnerable and the overall risk is critical: an unauthenticated SQL injection allows full database compromise, and global template auto-escaping is disabled enabling stored XSS. These are compounded by disabled CSRF protection, missing server-side authorization on state-changing endpoints, JavaScript-readable session cookies, and unsalted MD5 password hashing. Coverage was the entire repository except vendored static assets (materialize/jquery) and binary font files.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create via string-formatted INSERT
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the caller-supplied name directly into the SQL text instead of passing it as a query parameter. The only caller, the POST /students/ handler (sqli/views.py:54-57), takes name straight from request.post() and passes it unvalidated. That route (sqli/routes.py:14) has no authorization decorator, so any anonymous user can reach it. Because psycopg2/aiopg's execute allows multiple statements, an attacker can break out of the quoted value (e.g. name = x'); DROP TABLE marks; -- or a subquery/UNION) to read or destroy arbitrary data, including the users table with password hashes. This is the primary, fully-reachable vulnerability of the app.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  ->  await cur.execute(q). Source: views.students -> data['name'] (request.post()) -> Student.create(conn, data['name']).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query and let the driver bind the value: await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %-formatting or f-strings from user input.

findings.title: Global Jinja2 auto-escaping disabled enabling stored XSS
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so every template variable is rendered as raw HTML unless it carries an explicit | e filter. Many user-controlled values are printed without escaping: review.review_text (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22) which is created by the unauthenticated POST /courses/{id}/review endpoint, course.title/course.description (course.jinja2:14-15, courses.jinja2:17-18), student name (students.jinja2:16), and the logged-in user's names (base.jinja2:25). An attacker submitting a review containing <script> stores JavaScript that executes in every visitor's browser. Combined with the JavaScript-readable session cookie (see cookie finding) this yields session hijacking.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli','templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False). Sink example: course.jinja2 line 22 '{{ review.review_text }}' rendering attacker-supplied text with no escaping.
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the aiohttp_jinja2/Jinja2 default) and use the |safe filter only where HTML output is intentional and trusted. Remove the now-redundant manual | e filters or keep them as defense in depth.

findings.title: Missing server-side authorization on state-changing handlers (evaluate, create student/course)
findings.description: The evaluate handler creates marks with no authentication or authorization check, even though the UI exposes the form only to admins (course.jinja2:41 'if auth_user.is_admin'). Access control is enforced only by conditionally rendering forms in templates, which any HTTP client bypasses by POSTing directly. The same pattern affects POST /students/ (views.students, lines 54-57 -> create student, UI-gated to authenticated users) and POST /courses/ (views.courses, lines 86-90 -> create course, UI-gated to admins). None of these handlers, nor their routes (sqli/routes.py:14,18,22), use the existing @authorize decorator. Any anonymous user can create students/courses and assign marks to any student.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) with no get_auth_user/authorize call; contrast course.jinja2 line 41 which restricts the form to is_admin users. The authorize()/authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator exists in sqli/utils/auth.py:12 but is only applied to logout.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and courses, and @authorize() to students (or the appropriate role), enforcing the check in the handler rather than the template.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled application-wide
findings.description: The csrf_middleware that validates the per-session _csrf_token on POST requests (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) is commented out of the middleware chain, so no CSRF validation occurs even though templates embed csrf tokens. Every state-changing POST (login, add student, add course, submit review, evaluate, logout) can be triggered cross-site. An attacker can host a page that auto-submits a form to, e.g., /courses/{id}/review or /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} against an authenticated victim. The SameSite cookie flag is also not set (see cookie finding), so browsers do not mitigate this by default.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware] — csrf_middleware is present in the source but excluded from the active list.
findings.recommendation: Enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain, ensure it runs for all unsafe methods, and set SameSite=Lax/Strict on the session cookie as defense in depth.

findings.title: Session cookie readable by JavaScript (HttpOnly disabled)
findings.description: The Redis session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is exposed to client-side JavaScript. Given the stored-XSS exposure from disabled auto-escaping, an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session, taking over accounts including superadmin. No Secure or SameSite flag is configured either, so the cookie is also sent over plaintext and cross-site.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default), and set secure=True and samesite='Lax' on the session storage cookie.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 and compared non-constant-time
findings.description: check_password verifies credentials by comparing the stored hash to an unsalted MD5 of the supplied password. MD5 is fast and broken, and without a per-user salt the fixtures' hashes (migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13, e.g. md5('superadmin')) are trivially reversible via rainbow tables/GPU cracking. Any hashes leaked through the SQL injection above are effectively plaintext. The comparison also uses == which short-circuits and is not constant-time. This defines the app's password scheme, so it is the root cause for all stored credentials.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(); fixtures store pwd_hash as md5('superadmin') etc.
findings.recommendation: Hash passwords with a memory-hard KDF such as Argon2id or bcrypt (per-user salt built in) and verify with the library's constant-time verify function; migrate existing hashes on next login.

findings.title: aiohttp application runs with debug=True
findings.description: The Application is created with debug=True, which enables extra runtime checks and more verbose diagnostics. In a deployed environment this can aid attackers via more detailed error surfaces and slows the app. It should not be enabled outside local development. run.py also sets logging to DEBUG globally.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in non-development environments.

findings.title: Hardcoded database credentials in committed config
findings.description: The database username and password (postgres/postgres) are hardcoded in a committed config file, which is also the default config path used by the app (sqli/app.py:18). Committed default credentials are commonly reused and end up in production and version history. The Postgres port is also published to the host in docker-compose.yml:8-9.
findings.evidence:
db:
  user: postgres
  password: postgres
  host: postgres
findings.recommendation: Load secrets from environment variables or a secret manager, keep only non-secret defaults in committed config, and avoid publishing the database port to the host.
